title: How Python Actually Executes Your Code — Explained Visually

sentences: You type python, app dot py, press Enter, and a few milliseconds later, your program is running.
But what actually happened in between?
Is Python interpreted, or is it compiled?
The honest answer is: both. And by the end of this video, you'll see exactly how.
Most people describe Python as an interpreted language, as if something reads your text file line by line and simply obeys it.
That's not what happens.
In the standard implementation, called CPython, your source code is first compiled into a simpler instruction set called bytecode.
Then a program called the Python virtual machine executes that bytecode, one instruction at a time.
So CPython compiles, and then it interprets. Two phases, not one.
Here's the full journey of your code.
First, the tokenizer breaks your source text into tokens.
The parser arranges those tokens into a tree, called the abstract syntax tree.
The compiler walks that tree and emits bytecode, stored inside a code object.
Finally, the virtual machine runs the bytecode, and your program produces output.
Let's zoom into each stage.
Take a single line: total equals price times two.
The tokenizer splits it into five tokens: a name, an equals sign, another name, a star, and a number.
The parser then applies the grammar rules, and builds a tree.
At the top is an assignment. On the right side, a multiplication, with the name price on the left and the constant two on the right.
Notice that the tree captures meaning and structure, not just text. And syntax errors are caught right here, before any of your code runs.
Now the compiler turns that tree into bytecode.
Here's a tiny function that adds two numbers.
Using the built-in dis module, we can see its bytecode in Python three point twelve.
Load the variable a. Load the variable b. Add them with a binary operation. Return the result.
These instructions live in a code object, along with the constants and variable names the function needs.
And for imported modules, CPython caches this bytecode in dot pyc files, inside the pycache folder, so the next import can skip compilation.
Now the virtual machine takes over. It's a stack machine: instructions push and pop values on a stack.
Let's call add with two and three.
Load fast a pushes two onto the stack. Load fast b pushes three.
Binary op plus pops both values, adds them, and pushes the result: five.
Return value pops the five, and hands it back to the caller.
That loop, fetch an instruction, execute it, move to the next, is the heart of the interpreter.
But where do values actually live? In memory, as objects.
When you write x equals a list of one, two, three, Python doesn't put that list inside a box called x.
It creates a list object in memory, and binds the name x to it.
Now y equals x. No copy is made. Both names point at the same object.
The object keeps a reference count. Right now, it's two.
Change it through y, and x sees the change, because it's the same object. Reassign y to something else, and the count drops back to one.
When the count reaches zero, CPython frees the object immediately.
Objects that reference each other in cycles are cleaned up by a separate garbage collector.
Functions add one more idea: frames.
Every time you call a function, the interpreter creates a frame, holding that call's local variables and its place in the bytecode.
Calling a function from inside another function stacks a new frame on top.
When a function returns, its frame is removed, and execution continues in the caller.
This is exactly what you see in a traceback, and why runaway recursion ends with a RecursionError.
So why does any of this matter in real projects?
When code is slower than you expect, the dis module shows what the interpreter really executes.
Understanding references explains the classic bug where two variables unexpectedly change together, like when you share a list.
And the pycache folder explains why imports are faster the second time.

One last note: everything here describes CPython. Other implementations, like PyPy, add just-in-time compilation, and recent CPython versions optimize hot bytecode on the fly. The model stays the same. The details evolve.
Let's recap.
Python source is tokenized, parsed into a tree, compiled to bytecode, and executed by a virtual machine.
Variables are names bound to objects, and objects live as long as something references them.
Each function call gets its own frame on the call stack.
If this helped, subscribe, and tell me in the comments which system you want visualized next.
Is Python interpreted or compiled?
Both. And here's the proof.
First, CPython compiles your source code into bytecode.
You can see it yourself with the dis module.
Load a. Load b. Add. Return.
Then the Python virtual machine executes those instructions, one by one, using a stack.
Two goes on the stack. Three goes on the stack. Add pops both, and pushes five.
Compiled to bytecode, then interpreted by a virtual machine.
